bull_thesis: M6 is a well-run French broadcaster trading at roughly 11x price-to-free-cash-flow with net cash on the balance sheet, and the bull case has three legs. First, quality within a beaten-down group: M6 gains advertising share every quarter it reports (video advertising down about 3% in 2025 against a market down roughly 8%; first-half 2026 group advertising up about 1% against a market down roughly 9% excluding M6), on audience shares now at three-to-four-year highs across every key demographic. Second, a real digital transition: M6+ streaming grew about 26% to EUR 126 million in 2025 and is running ahead of its plan to reach EUR 200 million by 2028, now with 11 million active users and a new Amazon Prime distribution deal - the streaming leg is a genuine offset to linear decline, not vaporware. Third, and the biggest lever, consolidation optionality: the controlling shareholder, Bertelsmann's RTL Group (about 48% of M6), has openly said it hopes to revive a TF1-M6 merger, and a Senate-approved amendment would cut the license lock-up from five years to two, potentially freeing M6 for a deal by 2028. On a normalized earnings-power basis (through-cycle after-tax earnings around EUR 150-160 million capitalized at about 9.5-10x, plus EUR 110 million net cash) the business is worth roughly EUR 13 per share, and a consolidation/take-out scenario could carry it toward EUR 17. Net cash, a solvent balance sheet (Altman-Z 3.6), and a historically generous dividend cushion the downside while you wait. Conditions that must hold: the ad market must trough rather than keep sliding structurally, streaming must keep compounding, and the French media law must actually change.
bear_thesis: The optical cheapness is largely earned, not a gift. M6's earnings power has been in a multi-year structural fade - net income group share fell from EUR 281 million in 2021 to EUR 123 million in 2025 (a five-year earnings-per-share decline of about 18.5% a year), revenue is down about 2.6% a year over three years, and gross margin is contracting. 2026 is shaping up worse: first-half profit (EBITDA) fell about EUR 50 million, which management splits as half World Cup cost and half a deteriorating market, and the advertising market outside M6 is down roughly 9% with no called bottom. Management itself cannot say whether the ad decline is cyclical or structural - pressed hard by analysts, the CEO conceded it was 'difficult to answer.' The dividend, which underpins a substantially yield-driven shareholder base, was dodged twice in the July call ('too early to say'); a cut would trigger mechanical selling from income holders. The load-bearing upside - consolidation - is management lobbying, not a signed deal, and the identical TF1-M6 merger already collapsed in 2022 on antitrust remedies; the law change is only Senate-approved and must survive French political turbulence before the March municipal elections. Strip out the event optionality and, at EUR 12.10 against a normalized fair value near EUR 13, the margin of safety is thin single digits - you are not being paid much to own a melting-linear-TV base whose one durable growth engine (streaming) is not yet big enough to reverse the top line. What confirms the bear: a dividend cut, a fourth-quarter ad miss (World Cup spend pulled forward), or the media-law reform stalling.
consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power - and here the honest answer is that the market is roughly right, not wrong. The scan's own model spread is unusually wide and self-contradicting: a growth-style discounted-cash-flow model prints a EUR 23.5 fair value (over-extrapolating a recovery that a declining broadcaster will not deliver), while a Buffett-style capitalization prints EUR 6.0 (implying the stock is expensive) and the blended scan fair value is EUR 5.95 (a 47% overvaluation flag). That dispersion IS the signal: the value case is not clean - it hinges entirely on which normalization you believe. My reconciled base fair value of about EUR 13 sits just above the EUR 12.10 price, so the genuine expectations gap is thin. Where I do disagree with a lazy bear read: the street that dismisses M6 as a melting ice cube underrates the streaming transition (M6+ up ~26%, ahead of plan, audience share at multi-year highs) and the net-cash balance sheet - this is a transitioning franchise, not a liquidation. But where I refuse to disagree with the market: the durable upside requires a consolidation event that has already failed once and depends on a French law change, and no amount of quality reframing turns a thin single-digit margin of safety into a deep discount.
forcing_function: There is no hard, binding date. The re-rating triggers are, in ascending order of impact: (1) the French media-law amendment clearing full passage (beyond Senate approval) - the window is before the March 2026 municipal elections, so watch the first quarter of 2026 legislative calendar; (2) a formal TF1-M6 combination announcement or a Bertelsmann/RTL stake-sale process, which Bertelsmann's CEO has flagged for the next two-to-three years; (3) on the operating side, the FY2026 results in early 2027, where the dividend decision and the ad-market trough call will either confirm or refute the value thesis. None of these is a firm scheduled event with fixed terms - the consolidation path is a soft, non-binding, once-failed process contingent on legislation plus a controlling-shareholder decision plus antitrust clearance.
valley_of_death: The next three-to-nine months carry two dated, adverse pressure points. First, the dividend decision at the FY2026 results (early 2027): management dodged the payout question twice on the 28 July 2026 call ('too early to say… depending on cash flow and market results'), and 2026 is a down year - World Cup costs plus an advertising market off about 9% cut first-half EBITDA by roughly EUR 50 million. A cut or deferral is a live risk. Second, the fourth-quarter advertising print: analysts flagged that World Cup ad spend may have been pulled forward out of the traditionally-large fourth quarter, and management conceded 'there is both… hard to put a number on it' - so Q4 could disappoint even against easy optics. There is no debt-maturity wall (net cash EUR 110 million, Altman-Z 3.6), so this is an earnings-and-sentiment valley, not a solvency one; but a weak Q4 plus a dividend cut is exactly the sequence that takes the stock toward the adverse EUR 9-10 zone before any consolidation catalyst can land.
positioning_washout: The mechanical risk is concentrated in the shareholder base's yield orientation. M6 has historically paid a large dividend (a high-single-digit yield in prior years), which anchors an income-focused register of holders. Management's refusal to reaffirm the payout in a down-EBITDA, World Cup-hit 2026 is precisely the setup that forces income and passive-yield funds to liquidate mechanically if the dividend is cut - the payout, not the business quality, is what many of these holders own the stock for. That washout, if it comes, would likely be the better entry: a capitulation toward the 52-week low (EUR 11.02) or below would convert today's thin margin of safety into a real one. Offsetting this, Bertelsmann/RTL's ~48% control block is a stable, non-forced holder that will not sell into weakness - it wants a strategic exit at a premium, which caps how deep and durable a washout can be.
moderator_conclusion: M6 is a genuinely well-run, cash-rich, share-gaining French broadcaster that is nonetheless cheap for a reason: its earnings power has roughly halved since 2021, its gross margin is contracting, and 2026 is a down year from World Cup costs layered on an advertising recession. Against the current regime - dispersion, higher-for-longer rates, and an explicit preference for resolution-driver independence - two things matter. The thesis does NOT depend on rate cuts (good, it isn't penalized on that axis), but its durable upside DOES hinge on a single-binary political/regulatory driver (French media-law reform enabling consolidation) that has already collapsed once and is only Senate-approved - exactly the kind of one-shared-factor, non-binding catalyst the regime tells us to hold conditionally, not on faith. Reconciling the parts, base fair value is about EUR 13 against a EUR 12.10 price - a thin ~7% margin of safety - with an adverse case near EUR 9.5 (about -21%) and a consolidation bull case near EUR 17 (about +40%). That base-case skew is unattractive; you are paid little to wait and exposed to a dividend cut and a soft Q4 in the interim. This is a real thesis at not-yet-a-real-price: WATCHLIST. I would turn buyer on a specific development - the media-law amendment actually clearing the National Assembly, a formal consolidation/stake-sale process, OR a capitulation entry near the EUR 10.5 / 52-week-low area that converts the thin margin of safety into a genuine one. Separately, on value alone and ignoring the catalyst: the franchise is cheap-ish but the moat is eroding (falling returns, contracting margin) under a material linear-media-decline secular headwind, which caps the value score - a low multiple on a structurally-shrinking base with only single-digit downside protection is a moderate value case, not a deep one.
sop_breakdown: Base case, EUR per share (about 125.7 million shares): normalized after-tax earnings power of about EUR 150-155 million from the combined operations (linear M6/W9 television, M6+ streaming, RTL radio, production/audiovisual rights, diversification) capitalized at about 9.5x for a low-growth, structurally-declining but strongly cash-generative franchise = about EUR 1.45 billion (roughly EUR 11.5-12.0/share); plus a net-cash overlay of EUR 110 million (about EUR 0.9/share); rounding to a base fair value of about EUR 13.0. No clean segment EBITDA was disclosed, so the parts are illustrative: the video/streaming division is the dominant value (about 80% of revenue at roughly 16-17% margin), audio (RTL) is a stable high-margin contributor (about 24% EBITDA margin), production and diversification are smaller and lumpier. Consolidation is treated as upside optionality in the bull case, not embedded in the base.
risk_reward: Skewed unattractively in the base case, attractive only on the event. From EUR 12.10: downside to the adverse case (EUR 9.5) is about -21%; upside to base fair value (EUR 13.0) is only about +7%; upside to the consolidation/bull case (EUR 17.0) is about +40%. So on an event-free basis you risk roughly three units of downside for one of upside - you are being paid little to wait. The distribution is wide and bimodal: thin reward if nothing happens, large reward if consolidation fires, meaningful loss if the dividend is cut and the ad market keeps sliding. This is why the entry price and a hard legislative milestone matter more than the story.
peer_comps_note: Peer group: TF1 (TFI.PA, the closest comparable - same market, same free-to-air ad model), with ProSiebenSat.1 (PSM.DE), MFE/Mediaset (MFEA.MI) and ITV (ITV.L) as the pan-European cross-check. M6 screens at about 11.2x price-to-free-cash-flow versus TF1 at about 14.1x, despite better capital efficiency (ROIC 13.0% vs 9.4%) and a higher net margin (9.8% vs 6.7%) - so the specific discount to TF1 looks quality-justified and is a modest, defensible idiosyncratic edge. BUT the absolute low multiple across the whole cohort (ProSieben, MFE and ITV all similarly cheap) is SHARED-FACTOR sector beta: every name is being repriced on the same unresolved linear-TV advertising decline. I do NOT credit the cohort-wide cheapness as name-specific alpha - it is the sector's secular discount, and it will only compress if the shared driver (streaming displacement of linear ad spend) reverses, which it is not. Net: M6 is the better-quality name inside an already-cheap, structurally-challenged group; that supports a small relative premium to the group, not a re-rating to a healthy-media multiple.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Métropole Télévision S.A. (M6 Group), MMT.PA

*Interrogator note prepared for the investment committee. Ticker trades in Paris; all figures in euros unless stated. Live price EUR 12.10 (2026-08-02). Two earnings calls in evidence: full-year 2025 results (2026-02-17) and first-half 2026 results (2026-07-28).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

M6 is France's second free-to-air commercial broadcaster — the M6 and W9 television channels, the RTL family of radio stations, a film-and-television production arm, and a fast-growing streaming platform, M6+. The story management tells has shifted in emphasis across the two calls in a revealing way.

At the full-year 2025 call, the frame was "resilient decline managed well": advertising revenue was falling (video advertising down about 3.1% for the year), but M6 was outperforming a market it pegged at down roughly 8%, gaining video-advertising market share to about 27%. The growth engine on offer was M6+ streaming — revenue up 26% to EUR 126 million and, management stressed, ahead of the plan to reach EUR 200 million by 2028. Two forward promises anchored the call: an EUR 80 million cost-savings plan over five years (production, procurement, technical costs, partly enabled by using artificial intelligence in content production), and a lobbying campaign to modernise France's "obsolete" broadcasting law — above all the five-year rule that blocks consolidation.

By the first-half 2026 call the frame had narrowed to a single event: the FIFA World Cup, which M6 broadcast exclusively (54 matches). Management led with it for a reason — it was the good news. Audiences were extraordinary (a France–Spain semi-final peak above 20 million viewers, the second-best in the group's history), M6+ scaled hard (11 million active users, a chart-topping app), and the group was the number-one TV advertiser during the tournament. But underneath the trophy, the core deteriorated: first-half video-division profit (EBITDA) dropped about EUR 50 million, which management split as "half World Cup cost, half market." The advertising market excluding M6 fell about 9%. The growth driver quietly dropped between calls was any confidence on the dividend — dodged twice in the H1 Q&A.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Robust growth in streaming… slightly ahead of the milestones" (FY25) | M6+ revenue +26% to EUR 126M, on track for EUR 200M by 2028; group revenue still fell to EUR 1.26B (−4.3% YoY, −2.6% 3-yr CAGR) | **Matches, but doesn't rescue the top line.** Streaming is real and growing; it is not yet large enough to offset linear erosion. |
| "Strong profitability… EBITDA EUR 214M, 17% operating margin" (FY25) | Net income group share fell to EUR 123M (EPS EUR 0.98), down 27.9% YoY; 5-yr EPS CAGR −18.5% | **Poorer than the headline.** The margin is genuinely high for the peer group, but earnings power is on a multi-year decline (NI EUR 281M in 2021 → EUR 123M in 2025). |
| "We significantly outperformed the market" (both calls) | Video ad −3.1% (FY25) vs market −8%; H1-26 group ad +1% vs market ex-M6 −9% | **Matches.** Relative outperformance is verified and is the strongest part of the bull case — share gains at multi-year-high audiences. |
| "EBITDA effect of the World Cup in Q3 will be more or less zero" (H1-26) | H1 EBITDA −EUR 50M, half attributed to the tournament | **Plausible but self-serving.** The Q3 offset claim is unverifiable today; the H1 hit is booked and real. |
| Net cash / balance-sheet strength | Recomputed net cash EUR 110M (cash EUR 216M > total debt EUR 106M incl. leases) at 2025-12-31; Altman-Z 3.6 (solvent) | **Matches.** The balance sheet is a genuine strength and a real sum-of-the-parts add-back. |

The single most important divergence: management narrates a *cyclical* ad dip ("the level of this decrease is not justified… TV is a cheap medium"), while the financials show a *structural* five-year slide in revenue, earnings and gross margin (gross margin flagged "contracting"). Both can be true at once — a cyclical trough sitting on a secular downtrend — but the story is richer than the trajectory justifies.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining, with a defensive tilt.** In February the CEO was offensive: audience records, streaming milestones, a proactive cost plan, a reform agenda. By July the language turned protective — "the market is awfully complicated," "we have to be careful," "you need the right balance between defending audiences and defending our EBITDA." The most telling exchange was Bernstein's Christophe Cherblanc pressing on whether the video-ad market had "climbed down a flight of stairs that's going to be difficult to climb back up." The CEO's answer — "difficult to answer… I think this drop is not justified… but I'm not saying it's going to stop miraculously" — is an honest non-answer that concedes he cannot distinguish the cyclical from the structural. That is candour, but it is not confidence.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-to-High.** Where management set a hard, checkable target — the M6+ streaming ramp — they delivered and ran slightly ahead (EUR 126M, above plan; negative segment contribution −8% vs an expected −31%, i.e. better than feared). The EUR 80 million savings plan was framed honestly as gradual, not front-loaded. The earnings-beat rate in the screener is a coin-flip (1 of 2 quarters), and the recent quarterly EPS line is ugly (latest-quarter EPS down 57% YoY), so the credibility rests on the *strategic* promises being met rather than on quarterly precision. No sandbagging pattern; if anything they under-promised on streaming. Reliability on the controllable items: High. Reliability on the ad market: they explicitly decline to forecast it.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three pressure points recur, and management deflected all three. First, the **dividend** (Kepler's Conor O'Shea): asked directly whether a World Cup-hit, margin-down year would change the payout, the CEO said "it's difficult to know… too early to say" — twice. For a stock whose shareholder base is substantially yield-driven, that is the load-bearing dodge. Second, the **structural-vs-cyclical ad question** (Bernstein) — non-answered as above. Third, **pull-forward risk** (Deutsche Bank's Nizla Naizer): did World Cup ad money cannibalise the traditionally-large fourth quarter? The CEO conceded "there is both… hard to put a number on it." Each deflection sits exactly where the bear case lives.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Net income down 27.9% YoY to EUR 123M; 5-yr EPS CAGR −18.5% — a genuinely eroding earnings base.
🔴 Dividend guidance withdrawn in all but name — the yield support may not hold in a down 2026.
🔴 Gross margin "contracting"; ad market ex-M6 down ~9% with no called bottom.
🔴 The headline consolidation catalyst is management *lobbying*, not a signed deal — and the same TF1 merger already collapsed in 2022 on antitrust remedies.
🟢 Audience share at 3-to-4-year highs across every key demographic — the franchise is winning viewers even as the market shrinks.
🟢 M6+ streaming compounding ~26% and ahead of plan; the Amazon Prime distribution deal (new in H1-26) adds reach.
🟢 Net cash of about EUR 110 million and Altman-Z of 3.6 — no solvency risk, real optionality.
🟢 Consistent relative outperformance of the ad market in both up and down quarters.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The subtle tell is the pivot from "grow the business" to "reshape the industry." Across both calls the CEO spent unusual airtime on regulation — the five-year consolidation lock-up, advertising-sector prohibitions, DTT broadcast costs, radio music quotas. A management team that spends its prepared remarks lobbying for a law change is signalling that organic reinvestment alone will not fix the terminal-value problem; the exit it wants is *scale through consolidation*. Bertelsmann/RTL, which owns about 48% of M6, has said openly it hopes to revive a TF1–M6 merger within two-to-three years. Read together, the real thesis under the stock is not "cheap broadcaster compounds" — it is "cheap broadcaster gets consolidated or its stake sold, once the law allows." That is an event thesis wearing value clothing, and it has failed to fire once already.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** M6 is a well-run, cash-rich, share-gaining broadcaster whose underlying earnings power is nonetheless in a multi-year structural fade, with 2026 marked down further by World Cup costs and an ad recession.

The moat is an **intangible-brand plus regulatory-license** position (channel brands, DTT spectrum, audience habit) that is **NARROW and ERODING** — the evidence is falling returns (net income halved since 2021, EPS CAGR −18.5%) and a contracting gross margin, the textbook signature of an eroding, not widening, franchise. The secular force is **cord-cutting and streaming fragmentation of linear video and advertising** — the linear-media-decline theme. Crucially, I judge that threat **material, not terminal**: M6+ streaming is growing ~26% and heading for EUR 200M, audience share is at multi-year highs, and the balance sheet is net cash — this is a franchise *transitioning*, not one being liquidated. The optical cheapness (about 11x price-to-free-cash-flow) is therefore partly a fear-print and partly a fair discount for a shrinking base; it is not a clean mispricing.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** the upside beyond a thin single-digit margin of safety depends almost entirely on a *consolidation* event — a TF1 merger or a Bertelsmann stake sale — that requires a French law change (currently only Senate-approved, needing full passage amid political turbulence before the March municipal elections) and that has already failed once. Size this as a cheap-but-eroding franchise with real but soft, non-binding event optionality, not as a deep-value certainty.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: DETERIORATING | MOAT: ERODING | MOAT_TREND: ERODING | SECULAR_THREAT: material

bull_thesis: The bull case for M6 rests on three things that are all verifiably true, and on one thing that is not yet. First, this is the rare declining-media business that is genuinely winning its market. In 2025 the French video advertising market fell about 8%; M6's video advertising fell only 3.1% to 1,032 million euros of group advertising revenue, lifting its share of video advertising by 1.4 points to roughly 27%. In the first half of 2026 the gap widened to a chasm: group advertising rose about 1% while, on management's own figures given on the 28 July 2026 call, the market excluding M6 fell about 9% - a ten-point outperformance that took video advertising share to about 30%. The audience data behind it is real and improving: 2025 was the best group audience year in three, and the secondary channel W9 became the number-one digital terrestrial channel among 25-to-49-year-olds in the first half of 2026 with a 4.7% share, up 27%. Second, the digital transition is funded, tracked, and running ahead of its own plan. The M6+ streaming platform grew revenue 27% to 126 million euros in 2025 (up 73% in two years) against a stated target of 200 million euros, and its drag on profit came in at minus 8% versus a planned minus 31% because viewing grew faster than the cost base. The 2026 World Cup added four million new accounts, eleven million active users and 100 million hours viewed, and made M6+ the most-downloaded application in France during the tournament. A new Amazon Prime distribution deal extends the reach further. Alongside it sits an under-appreciated audio franchise: the number-one radio station in France, a 24.4% profit margin, the second-largest commercial podcast publisher with 39 million monthly listens and seven of the country's top thirty podcasts. Third, there is a quantified self-help lever. In February 2026 management announced 80 million euros of savings over five years against a roughly one-billion-euro cost base, split about half programming and half other costs, with no meaningful restructuring charge attached - they intend to renegotiate with producers rather than fire people. They have form: 25.4 million euros of linear cost savings were delivered in 2025 while streaming investment continued. The balance sheet supports the wait, with net debt of about 65 million euros including leases against roughly 200 million euros of annual profit before depreciation - about 0.3 times, the least levered position in the European broadcast cohort. The thing that is not yet true is the re-rating trigger. The chief executive has made repeal of France's 'five-year rule', which blocks consolidation of the domestic broadcast market, the centrepiece of a six-point regulatory campaign: 'When you see what's going on in the U.S., it is ridiculous what we have in France. I hope that we'll be able to change the law in the months to come' (17 February 2026). If that law changes, a market with too many channels chasing a shrinking advertising pool consolidates, and M6 - a scaled, near-unlevered, controlled asset with the best audience momentum in the sector - is either the buyer or the prize. The conditions the bull case requires: the French advertising market must stop falling at high single digits; the 80-million-euro savings plan must land without buying it back in lost ratings; streaming must reach its 200-million-euro target at a positive margin; and the board must hold a dividend that the 2025 cash flow did not cover.
bear_thesis: The bear case is simpler and it is mostly arithmetic. M6's revenue has fallen for four consecutive years, from 1.39 billion euros in 2021 to 1.26 billion in 2025, and earnings per share have compounded at minus 18.5% over five years, from 2.22 euros in 2021 to 0.98 in 2025. The first half of 2026 is the cleanest possible illustration of why market-share wins do not fix this: revenue grew 4.1% to 643.8 million euros on the back of the World Cup, and profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation still fell 34.7%, to 87.8 million euros from 134.5 million. Net income fell to 36.3 million euros from 64.2 million; earnings per share to 0.29 euros from 0.51. Management attributes about half of that fall to the tournament, which is one-off - but that leaves roughly 25 million euros attributed to 'the market effect', and that half recurs every period until the French advertising market stops shrinking. Asked directly on 28 July 2026 whether France had permanently stepped down a level, the chief executive could not say: 'difficult to know which has had which impact, very difficult to do', before asserting that the decline 'is not justified'. An advertising market falling 9% with no recession to explain it is the textbook signature of a structural, not cyclical, migration - and the same generative-artificial-intelligence tooling management is counting on to cut its production costs is simultaneously collapsing the cost of the digital inventory that competes with its airtime. The returns confirm the erosion: return on invested capital has roughly halved from about 13% to about 7.7% on a trailing basis; return on equity from about 15.7% to about 8.2%; gross margin is contracting; the operating margin sits about two standard deviations below its historical peak; and the largest division's margin fell to 16.6% from 17.4% in 2025 and fell again in the first half of 2026. Then there is the payout. M6 has paid 1.25 euros a share for three consecutive years - most recently ex-dividend on 4 May 2026, paid 6 May 2026 - costing about 157 million euros a year against 2025 free cash flow of 126.4 million. The consequence is visible on the balance sheet: cash of 443.9 million euros at the end of 2023, 332 million at the end of 2024, 216 million at the end of 2025, and 33 million at 30 June 2026 against 88 million of borrowings and about 10 million of leases. In eighteen months a company with a large net cash pile became one with about 65 million euros of net debt. Consensus has 2026 earnings per share at 0.89 euros; the dividend is 140% of that. When asked in July whether the payout would follow the margin decline, management said only that it was 'too early to say'. Finally, and decisively, the price does not compensate. On live trailing figures the shares change hands at about 7.0 times enterprise value to profit before depreciation - roughly 6.3 times adding back the World Cup drag - against 2.1 times for TF1, 4.2 times for ProSiebenSat.1 and 5.9 times for ITV. On enterprise value to sales M6 is the most expensive of the five names in its comparison group. The stock sits about 1% above its 200-day average and roughly 42% up its 52-week range: there has been no capitulation, no forced sale, and no discount to pay for the structural risk. What would confirm the bear case: a dividend cut at the full-year results, a fourth-quarter advertising season that reveals World Cup budget pull-forward, or a 2027 in which the savings plan is fully consumed by further advertising decline.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not the usual direction for a cheap-looking stock. The standard case here is that the street is pricing terminal decline into a business with stable earnings power. I think the opposite is happening: the street is pricing a recovery into a business whose earnings power is still falling. The specific assumption I believe is wrong is the 2027 forecast. Six analysts covering this name model 2027 revenue of about 1,248 million euros and profit before depreciation of about 245 million euros, with earnings per share of 1.23 - against 2026 estimates of 180 million euros and 0.89, and against the 214 million euros the company actually delivered in 2025. In other words, consensus expects 2027 profit to land roughly 15% above the 2025 level and about 36% above 2026, and holds it there through 2028 at 248 million euros. That requires three things to happen at once: the World Cup cost disappears (fair - it will), the 80-million-euro savings plan delivers meaningfully (possible, but it is spread over five years and depends on renegotiating terms with external producers, which management conceded is 'an industrial process' with 'a progressive ramp-up'), and the French advertising market stops falling. That last one is the load-bearing assumption and nobody has evidence for it - least of all management, who declined to forecast the market in February 2026 and could not diagnose it in July. The market fell about 8% in 2025 and about 9% excluding M6 in the first half of 2026, in an economy that is not in recession. The second wrong assumption is embedded in the price rather than the models: at 12.06 euros the shares trade on about 9.8 times the 2027 consensus and about 6.8 times consensus 2027 profit before depreciation, when the directly comparable French broadcaster changes hands at 2.1 times trailing profit and the German one at 4.2 times. The market is not treating M6 as a melting asset; it is treating it as a cyclical due a bounce, with an income kicker. The third assumption is the dividend. A 1.25-euro payout against 0.89 euros of consensus 2026 earnings is a 140% distribution, and 2025's payout of 157 million euros already exceeded free cash flow of 126 million while the cash balance fell from 216 million euros to 33 million by mid-year. Anyone owning this for a 10% yield is underwriting a payout the cash flow statement has already stopped supporting. Our disagreement, in one line: the market thinks it is buying an out-of-favour cyclical at a discount; on our numbers it is paying a premium to the sector for a structurally shrinking base.
forcing_function: The one dated event that matters is the full-year 2026 results in mid-February 2027 - about five and a half months out - where the board proposes the dividend. The company reported on 17 February 2026, 11 February 2025 and 13 February 2024, so the timing is reliable even though the exact date is not yet confirmed, and management pointed at it directly on 28 July 2026: 'we'll see, depending on the cash flow position and the market results at the end of the year.' That single decision resolves the largest open question in the shares. Hold the 1.25 euros and management signals confidence in 2027 cash generation, and the income holders stay; cut it and the yield-driven part of the register is forced out, which is the point at which this name becomes genuinely interesting to a value buyer. Either way it forces a re-rating, and today's price does not discriminate between the two outcomes. The second forcing function is the one the bulls are actually waiting for - a change to French law repealing the rule that blocks domestic broadcast consolidation, which would unlock either a merger or a bid for a scaled, controlled, near-unlevered asset. That has no date, no binding commitment and no verifiable legislative step in the materials available to me; it is a hope expressed by a chief executive in February 2026, not an event on a calendar. # Forensic Dossier — Métropole Télévision S.A. (M6 Group), Euronext Paris: MMT.PA

**Prepared:** 2026-08-31 · **Price used:** EUR 12.06 (Euronext Paris, quote currency EUR; last trade, market capitalisation about EUR 1.52 billion on roughly 126.4 million shares) · **Transcripts available:** two calls only — full-year 2025 results (2026-02-17) and first-half 2026 results (2026-07-28), both supplied with the middle of the call omitted. The narrative arc below is therefore drawn from two data points, not eight, and I flag where that limits the read.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

M6 is France's second commercial broadcaster: four free-to-air television channels (M6, W9, 6ter, Gulli), a streaming platform (M6+), the country's leading radio group (RTL, RTL2, Fun Radio), a production and film-rights arm, and a small "diversification" cluster of franchised retail, kids' play parks and minority stakes in digital-marketing businesses.

Across the two calls the story has not shifted so much as it has narrowed and hardened. In February 2026, chief executive David Larramendy opened on profitability and audience — "only 2 figures to remember. That was a good year with an EBITDA of EUR 214 million for a current operating margin of 17%" — and framed 2025 as a year of successful transformation: streaming revenue up 27% to EUR 126 million, best group audience in three years, prime-time ratings ratio against the main competitor at 76%, "something that hasn't been achieved in the 2020s."

By July 2026 the emphasis had moved decisively to two things that were barely present in February: an event (the football World Cup, of which M6 was the sole French broadcaster for 54 matches between 11 June and 19 July 2026) and the advertising market itself. The bragging is now relative rather than absolute — the group's advertising revenue rose about 1% in the first half while, on management's own numbers, "if you look at the market, excluding M6 Group, it's at more or less minus 9%."

Three drivers have been introduced over the two calls:

1. **A cost programme.** In February management announced EUR 80 million of savings over five years across a roughly EUR 1 billion cost base, split about half programming and half everything else, with artificial intelligence in production explicitly named as an enabler.
2. **A regulatory campaign.** Six specific asks, led by repeal of the "5-year rule" that blocks consolidation of the French broadcast market. Larramendy: "When you see what's going on in the U.S., it is ridiculous what we have in France. I hope that we'll be able to change the law in the months to come."
3. **Third-party distribution.** A partnership with Amazon Prime to carry M6 content, disclosed in July, which was not part of the February story.

Nothing material has been quietly dropped, which is to management's credit — the streaming milestones set at the start are still reported against, and the shortfall areas (diversification profit, production and rights) are named rather than buried. What has changed is the tone about the core. In February the advertising decline was presented as an outperformance story; by July the chief executive was being asked directly whether France has "climbed down a ladder or a flight of stairs, that's going to be difficult to climb up again," and his answer was notably unresolved.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The pattern here is consistent and important: every claim management makes about audience, share and streaming is true; none of it has yet stopped the earnings base from shrinking.

| Management claim | Where it appears | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "A good year with an EBITDA of EUR 214 million... margin of 17%" | Feb 2026 | Correct, but full-year 2025 revenue fell 4.3% to EUR 1.256 billion and net income fell to EUR 123 million from EUR 173 million. Earnings per share of EUR 0.98 was down 27.9% year on year, and the five-year earnings-per-share compound growth rate is −18.5%. | True but selectively framed |
| Video advertising down only 3.1% against a market down 8%; share up 1.4 points to about 27% | Feb 2026 | Consistent with revenue falling less than the market. But relative outperformance in a shrinking market still produces an absolute decline: three-year revenue compound growth is −2.6%. | Verified; not value-creating on its own |
| Streaming "robust growth", EUR 126 million, up 27% | Feb 2026 | Real, and running slightly ahead of the company's own plan: the 2025 contribution drag was −8% against a planned −31%, and cumulative operating spend is below the EUR 80 million pencilled in for the early years. But EUR 126 million is only about 10% of group revenue, off a base that must reach EUR 200 million to offset a fraction of the linear decline. | Verified; under-scaled |
| First-half 2026 advertising up about 1% against a market down about 9% | Jul 2026 | First-half revenue was EUR 643.8 million, up 4.1% on the EUR 618.2 million of a year earlier — so the top line genuinely grew. | Verified |

Net income fell to EUR 36.3 million from EUR 64.2 million; earnings per share to EUR 0.29 from EUR 0.51. The split is plausible, but it means roughly EUR 25 million of the fall is not the World Cup and does not come back. | Verified, with the uncomfortable half understated |
| The advertising decline "is not justified... TV channels are a cheap medium" | Jul 2026 | An opinion contradicted by four consecutive years of revenue erosion (EUR 1.39 billion in 2021 to EUR 1.26 billion in 2025) and by margin data: gross margin is contracting and the operating margin sits about 1.95 standard deviations below its historical peak. | Narrative richer than the trajectory justifies |

The group paid EUR 157.1 million of dividends in 2025 — roughly EUR 1.24 per share — against free cash flow of EUR 126.4 million.
